title: Constrained Hand Dynamics: Motion, Contact, And Internal Force
notes: Open by naming the split that will organize the lecture: the hand must move the object, satisfy rolling or contact constraints, and regulate forces that do not show up as object motion. Students should hear that dynamics and control are being built on the constraint geometry from earlier grasping chapters, not replacing it.

title: From Constraints To Allowed Velocities
notes: Use the figure as the first inspection object. Ask students to point to the allowed direction before reading the formula. Then connect the drawing to A(q) dot q equals zero: each row is a covector that tests velocity, and the hand is allowed to use only the velocities that pass all tests simultaneously.

title: Lagrange Multipliers As Constraint Forces
notes: This slide is the bridge from kinematic restrictions to dynamics. Emphasize that lambda is determined by enforcing the acceleration-level constraint, while A transpose lambda lies in generalized force coordinates. The plane picture also prepares d'Alembert's principle: these reaction forces are orthogonal to every allowed virtual displacement.

title: d'Alembert Projection
notes: Do not rush the notation here. First say the geometric sentence: allowed virtual motions cannot detect ideal constraint forces. Then show how the nullspace basis N_A turns that sentence into equations. This is why projection is a modeling step, not merely algebraic cleanup after solving for multipliers.

title: Rolling Disk Split
notes: Use the disk because it is less visually crowded than a hand and still contains the important issue. The first equation forbids sideways motion, while the second couples rolling distance to spin. Once theta changes, the allowed direction in the plane changes, which is the seed of the nonholonomic behavior on the next slide.

title: The Nonholonomic Failure Mode
notes: Name the mistake explicitly because it is attractive in calculations. Students may want to integrate every row of A into a lost coordinate. The loop diagram shows why that is dangerous: legal small motions can compose into a displacement that no single position constraint would predict. This matters for rolling fingers as much as for wheels.

title: Composite Hand-Object Dynamics
notes: The essential teaching point is that contact coupling is not an afterthought. If the fingers and object are modeled separately and patched together later, the constraint forces become mysterious. The composite equation says where every coordinate lives and where lambda enters, so later control laws can be checked for dimensional and physical consistency.

title: Structural Lemma For Control
notes: Present this as a structural lemma rather than a new modeling assumption. The payoff is that the controller can use familiar manipulator tools after constraints are handled correctly. The caveat is equally important: the reduced coordinates and projected inputs carry the contact geometry, so hiding the projection hides the assumptions that make the controller valid.

title: Internal Forces Are Nullspace Forces
notes: Keep the algebra tied to the picture. The grasp map sends contact forces to an object wrench, so its nullspace contains contact force patterns the object cannot feel as a net wrench. Those patterns are not wasted effort: they maintain grip margin, preload rolling contacts, and prepare the hand to reject disturbances without changing the commanded motion.

title: Other Constrained Robot Systems
notes: This slide stays inside the chapter's Section 2.3 examples. Coordinated lifting shows several manipulators sharing one object equation. Workspace dynamics show how the Jacobian moves the same structure into task coordinates. Hybrid control separates tangent motion from normal force regulation. The common habit is not a generic constraint slogan; it is the specific hand-object equation reused in nearby robot systems.

title: Redundancy: Motions Invisible To The Task
notes: Connect this to internal forces without conflating them. Internal force nullspaces live in contact force coordinates; redundancy nullspaces live in motion coordinates. A dexterous hand often has both, and a controller has to decide how to spend them: keep the object tracking, improve the grasp geometry, and avoid joint or contact limits.

title: Nonmanipulable Grasps Restrict Object Motion
notes: Slow down on the distinction between holding and manipulating. A nonmanipulable grasp may resist some external wrenches and still lack enough independent motion directions to steer the object locally. This is where rank is not abstract linear algebra; it is the difference between a controller target that is reachable and one that asks for motion the contacts cannot provide.

title: Tendon Extension Becomes Torque Coupling
notes: Treat tendon actuation as another map between spaces. The same virtual-work logic used for contact forces now explains why R transpose maps tension into generalized torque. The asymmetry is crucial: motors at joints can often be idealized as signed torques, while tendons impose pull-only feasibility and couple joints through their routing.

title: Elastic Tendons And Force Closure
notes: Use the artifact to make feasibility visible. The tendon matrix may span useful torque directions, but the nonnegative tension requirement clips that span to a cone. Elasticity helps by keeping tension positive and by storing preload, yet it does not erase the cone test. Force closure must be checked against the actual actuation model.

title: Tracking Plus Internal Force Regulation
notes: Frame the displayed law as a shape rather than a prescription for one implementation. The important point is compositional: object tracking, commanded wrench, internal squeeze, and posture objectives enter through maps that respect contact constraints. If any term is added in the wrong coordinate space, the controller may fight the constraints instead of using them.

title: Hierarchical Control As Geometry-Aware Composition
notes: Close by returning to the hierarchy rather than a single formula. The chapter's control story is geometry-aware composition: constraints first, projected dynamics second, task and internal-force objectives third, and actuator feasibility last. That order is not bookkeeping. It is what prevents the hand from commanding beautiful object motion that violates contact, friction, or tendon limits.
